_readme: Three YouTube uploads for an AI tools & automation channel. Each has a long-form video (Google Flow clips + pyxa.ai voiceover) and a companion Short. Consumed by Claude Code running locally on the PC, which assembles the clips. See ASSEMBLY-BRIEF.md in the same folder.

channel.subject: AI tools, automation, agentic workflows
channel.audience: technical enough to build, short on time - wants architecture and failure modes, not feature tours
channel.tone: calm authority. Never hype. Describing something you built, to someone who will build it too.
channel.visual_style: isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed
channel.hard_rule: Never ask any generator for a screen, dashboard, code editor or app window - it cannot render a real UI and will produce garbled nonsense. Represent software as physical mechanism: pipelines, valves, node graphs, chambers, vaults, filtration, flowing light.

audio_direction.flow_native_audio: Let Flow generate ambient sound design only - mechanical hum, tonal resonance, room tone. Every flow_prompt ends with an explicit audio instruction that excludes speech and music.
audio_direction.why_no_speech: Flow will invent dialogue if you let it. That collides with the pyxa.ai voiceover and there is no way to separate them after generation. Exclude it in the prompt, not in the edit.
audio_direction.why_no_music: Flow's music cannot be beat-matched across clips and will jump at every cut. Add one continuous music bed in the edit instead.
audio_direction.voiceover: pyxa.ai reads the 'narration' field of each scene, in order. One render per scene keeps timing controllable.
audio_direction.music_bed: One continuous track under the whole video at low level. Direction per upload in 'music_direction'.

youtube.title: I Built an AI That Makes My YouTube Videos For Me
youtube.description:
This video was made by the system it describes. One line of text goes in. A finished video comes out the other end - script, visuals, voice, music, all of it.

Here's the architecture, why it's built on a strict data contract instead of loose text, and the one safety valve that stops it publishing garbage while I'm asleep.

CHAPTERS
0:00 This video made itself
0:22 The problem with making content by hand
1:00 The architecture, end to end
1:24 Why the AI must return strict data
2:02 Running a week of content in one go
2:20 The safety valve
3:18 What it costs and what it cannot do

THE STACK
Google Flow for the visuals
pyxa.ai for the voiceover
A language model for the script and the routing contract
Assembled locally, uploaded private, reviewed before release

The most important design decision is in chapter 4. Everything else is plumbing.

#AI #Automation #AIAutomation #ContentCreation #NoCode

scenes.narration: This video was made by the system it is about. I wrote one line of text. Everything after that - the script you are hearing, the images you are looking at, the music underneath, and the upload itself - was generated and assembled without me touching it. I want to show you exactly how it works, because the interesting part is not the AI. It is the shape of the thing around the AI.

scenes.narration: Making a video by hand takes hours. Write the script. Find the visuals. Record the voice. Cut it together. Every one of those is a separate app and a separate context switch, and the cost is not the individual step. It is that you have to be present for all of them, in order, every single time.

Camera: slow lateral truck left to right across the gaps. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: So the goal was never to make the AI more creative. It was to remove myself from the middle of it. One input at the front, one finished artifact at the back, and no human required in between unless something goes wrong.
scenes.flow_prompt: A clean sealed pipeline crossing the frame with one entry port and one exit port, warm light pulsing through it steadily from one end to the other. scenes.narration: Here is the shape. A brief goes into a language model that acts as a creative director. It does not write the video. It writes the instructions for four other systems - what to say, what to show, what it should sound like, and how to cut it. Those four run in parallel. An assembler stitches the results. The uploader publishes it.
scenes.flow_prompt: An isometric node graph where a single input node branches into four parallel processing nodes that each pulse in turn, then converge into one output node, glowing connection lines carrying light along each path. Camera: slow orbit around the graph, revealing depth. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: The critical decision is that the creative director does not return prose. It returns a strict data structure with exactly four fields. Not a description of what should happen. A machine-readable object where every field has exactly one destination.
scenes.flow_prompt: A precisely machined metal block with four distinct keyed slots of different shapes, each slot lit a different colour, four matching components hovering above and lowering into place. Camera: slow push in on the block as the components seat. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: That matters more than it sounds. If the model returns friendly prose, something downstream has to parse it, and that parser breaks the first time the model gets chatty. A strict contract means the routing is dumb. Field one goes here. Field two goes there. Dumb routing is reliable routing.
scenes.flow_prompt: Four separate coloured streams of light flow from a single junction into four distinct receptacles without ever crossing or mixing, perfectly ordered separation. Camera: static overhead shot looking down on the junction. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Once one brief works, a queue works. Paste in five briefs. A loop feeds them through one at a time, waits for each to finish, then advances. A week of content from one run, while I am doing something else entirely.
scenes.flow_prompt: A carousel mechanism advances identical glowing capsules one at a time into a processing chamber, a queue of further capsules waiting behind receding into soft focus. Camera: slow tracking shot alongside the queue toward the chamber. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: But batching is exactly where this gets dangerous, so there is a valve. Before anything expensive runs, a check asks one question - does the output actually contain all four required fields. If yes, continue. If no, stop this one, log it, move to the next.
scenes.flow_prompt: A precision gate valve mid-pipeline opens and closes decisively, one path beyond it brightly lit and flowing, the other sealed and dimmed. Camera: static medium shot on the valve mechanism as it actuates. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: That check exists because language models occasionally return malformed output, especially when you have turned the creativity up. Without the valve, one bad generation burns image credits, voice credits, music credits and a full render before anyone notices. With it, the bad one costs nothing.
scenes.flow_prompt: Inside a dark chamber a single visibly faulty component is diverted sideways into a containment tray while the main line of identical good components continues past undisturbed. Camera: slow push in following the faulty component as it diverts. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: And every upload lands as private. Never public. The system builds the video, files it away, and stops. I review the batch, and I decide what goes out. Automation that publishes unattended is not a workflow. It is a liability with a schedule attached.
scenes.flow_prompt: A row of sealed containers on a dark shelf each glowing softly from within, one of them lifted and opened by a human silhouette lit in warm light. Camera: slow pull back from the opened container to reveal the full row. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: The honest limits. It cannot show a real screen recording, because generated visuals cannot render a real interface. It cannot fact-check itself. And it has no taste - it will produce the mediocre version forever unless the brief is good. The system removed the labour. It did not remove the judgement.

scenes.narration: If you want the architecture, the field contract, and the validation rule, they are in the description. Build the valve first. Everything else is easier to fix than a pipeline that fails silently and expensively.

youtube.title: This Folder Runs an AI Workflow Every Time I Drop a File In It
youtube.description:
No dashboard. No button. I drop a file into a folder and two minutes later the work is done and an email is waiting for me.

This is the heartbeat pattern - a timer that wakes up, looks for new work, and does it. It is the simplest automation trigger there is and it replaces most of what people build buttons for.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Drop a file, walk away
0:20 Why polling beats a button
0:40 How the heartbeat actually works
1:00 Marking work as done (the bug everyone hits)
1:40 Chaining two AI models back to back
2:18 Where I put the guardrail
2:58 What this pattern is bad at

THE PATTERN
A timer fires every 2 minutes
It scans a folder for files it has not seen
For each new file it runs the work and marks the file processed
It emails when the result is ready

The processed-list step in chapter 4 is the one everybody forgets, and it will re-run your entire folder until you add it.

#AI #Automation #AIAutomation #NoCode #Workflow

uploads.music_direction: downtempo electronica, around 96 BPM, soft rhodes chords, muted kick, warm sub bass. Calm and patient with space in it.

scenes.narration: I put a file in a folder. That is the entire interface. Two minutes later the work is finished and there is an email waiting. No dashboard, no button, no app open. The folder is the trigger, and the pattern behind it is the most useful automation idea I know.
scenes.flow_prompt: A single small object is placed into a softly glowing recess in a dark surface and rings of light ripple outward from the point of contact. Camera: slow push in toward the recess as the ripples spread. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Most people build a button. A button means you have to be there, in the right app, at the right moment. But the work does not arrive on a schedule - it arrives when you happen to have the idea. So the trigger should be the act of saving the file, not the act of pressing anything.
scenes.flow_prompt: A single pristine illuminated button sits untouched on a pedestal while a fast bright stream of activity rushes past it in the background, never intersecting. Camera: static locked-off shot, button sharp in foreground, stream blurred behind. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: The mechanism is almost stupidly simple. A timer fires every two minutes. It wakes up, looks in a specific folder, and asks one question - is there anything here I have not seen before. Almost every time the answer is no, and it goes back to sleep costing nothing.
scenes.flow_prompt: A single pulse of light travels slowly around a closed circular circuit in a dark chamber at a patient steady rhythm, the rest of the frame at rest. Camera: slow orbit around the circuit following the pulse. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: When the answer is yes, it takes that file and starts the work. And this is where the bug lives that everybody hits at least once. If you do not record that you have processed the file, the next heartbeat finds it again. And the next one. You do not get one run. You get a run every two minutes, forever, until you notice the bill.
scenes.flow_prompt: A loop of light doubles back on itself and retraces the same segment over and over, each pass adding brightness until one point of the loop is uncomfortably overexposed. Camera: slow push in on the overheating point as it brightens. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: So the last thing every run does is add that file to a processed list. Small step, easy to skip, and it is the difference between an automation and a runaway. Test it by dropping in one file and watching for the second email that should never come.
scenes.flow_prompt: A mechanical counter advances one notch with a decisive movement and a completed component slides into a separate sealed compartment. Camera: static close shot on the counter and compartment. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Now the useful part - what happens between detection and delivery. I chain two models. The first one cleans and structures the raw input, because what I dump into a folder at midnight is not a well-formed prompt. It is a fragment.
scenes.flow_prompt: A rough irregular shard travels into a refining chamber and emerges from the other side as a clean precise geometric form. Camera: slow lateral tracking shot following the shard through the chamber. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: The second model does the actual generation, working from that cleaned structure instead of my half-formed note. Two cheap calls in sequence beat one expensive call on bad input, every time. Garbage in, garbage out is not a saying about AI. It is a description of where to put your effort.
scenes.flow_prompt: Two chambers connected in series, material passing from the first into the second and emerging noticeably brighter and more resolved than it entered. Camera: slow dolly following the material left to right through both chambers. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Between those two steps sits a sanitiser. Before anything leaves my machine for a cloud model, it strips the things I have decided do not go to third-party AI. That list is mine and it is not up for negotiation by the automation.
scenes.flow_prompt: A fine filtration membrane spans a pipeline, certain glowing particles caught and settling against it while the rest pass cleanly through into brighter space beyond. Camera: static medium shot on the membrane, particles collecting. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: That is worth saying plainly. The moment you automate a pipeline, you stop reading what goes through it. Whatever rule you would have applied by hand has to become a step in the chain, before the send, or it stops existing at all.
scenes.flow_prompt: A guarded threshold in a dark corridor, warm private light on one side and cold open space on the other, a hard bright boundary line between them. Camera: slow push toward the threshold, stopping short of crossing it. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: What is this pattern bad at? Anything urgent. A two minute poll means a two minute wait, and tightening it to ten seconds multiplies your invocations for almost no benefit. It is also bad at anything needing a human decision partway through - the moment it has to stop and ask, the whole advantage evaporates.
scenes.flow_prompt: A precise mechanism turns steadily at a measured unhurried pace inside its enclosure while outside a fast blurred stream rushes past in the opposite direction. Camera: static shot, sharp slow mechanism centre frame, motion-blurred rush behind. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: But for work that arrives unpredictably and can wait a couple of minutes, it is close to perfect. Drop the file. Close the laptop. The email arrives when it arrives.

youtube.title: One Keyword In, a Full Research Report Out - Built in an Afternoon
youtube.description:
I type one word. A few seconds later I have a structured research report I would otherwise have spent an afternoon assembling.

Three moving parts, one of which most tutorials skip and then wonder why their automation dies in production.

CHAPTERS
0:00 One word in, a report out
0:20 The three parts
0:38 Why the webhook goes in the middle
1:18 The prompt is the actual product
2:00 Structured output beats a wall of text
2:20 The failure everyone hits in production
3:02 What I would not use this for

THE SHAPE
A trigger sends one keyword to a webhook
The webhook calls a language model with a long, specific prompt
The response comes back structured, not as prose
The result renders where you asked for it

Chapter 4 is the one that matters. A generic prompt gives you a generic report, and a generic report is worse than no report because you will act on it.

#AI #Automation #AIAutomation #Research #NoCode

scenes.narration: I type a single word. A few seconds later I have a structured report - the landscape, who is doing what, where the gaps are. Work that used to be an afternoon of tabs. Three moving parts make it happen, and one of them is the part most tutorials skip.
scenes.flow_prompt: A single small seed of light drops into a dark still reservoir and expands outward into an intricate ordered lattice of connected glowing points. Camera: slow rise from water level to overhead as the lattice spreads. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Part one is the trigger - anything that can send text. Part two is a webhook, which is just a URL that waits. Part three is the language model that does the thinking. That is the whole architecture. The complexity is not in the wiring.
scenes.flow_prompt: Three distinct mechanical modules of different shapes connected in a line by glowing conduits, light passing from the first through to the third. Camera: slow lateral truck along the line of modules. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: The webhook sits in the middle for one reason - it decouples the two ends. The thing that sends the keyword does not need to know anything about the model, the credentials, or the prompt. Change the model later and the front end never notices.
scenes.flow_prompt: A central rotating coupling joins two independent shafts, one side turning freely while the other remains still, precise engineering tolerance visible. Camera: slow orbit around the coupling. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Which means your API key lives in exactly one place, server side, never in the thing you are typing into. If you are building this and your key is sitting in the front end, stop and move it. That is not a style preference. That is the whole reason the middle layer exists.
scenes.flow_prompt: A single glowing key sealed inside an armoured vault at the centre of a system, conduits radiating outward from the vault carrying light but never carrying the key. Camera: slow push in through the conduits toward the sealed vault. isometric technical illustration style, dark slate and deep navy palette, cyan and warm amber accent glow, clean matte 3D render, soft volumetric lighting, no text, no letters, no numbers, no signage, no UI, cinematic, highly detailed. Audio: ambient sound design only: low mechanical hum and soft tonal resonance. No speech, no voices, no dialogue, no music.

scenes.narration: Now the part that actually determines whether this is useful. The prompt. Not the model, not the platform - the prompt. A vague prompt returns a confident, generic, useless report, and a generic report is worse than no report, because you will act on it.

scenes.narration: So mine is long and specific. It names the exact sections I want. It says who the reader is. It says what to do when the model does not know something, which is to say so rather than invent. And it fixes the output shape, so every report comes back looking the same.

scenes.narration: That last one matters more than it sounds. Ask for prose and you get a wall of text you have to read end to end. Ask for a defined structure and you get something you can scan in fifteen seconds, compare against last week, and feed into the next step automatically.

scenes.narration: Here is the failure everyone hits in production. It works perfectly ten times, then returns something malformed - a truncated response, an extra sentence wrapped around the output, a field missing. If the next step assumes the response is well-formed, the whole chain breaks at the worst moment.

scenes.narration: So validate before you use it. Check the response actually contains what you asked for. If it does, continue. If it does not, stop that run and log it. Ten lines of checking, and it is the difference between an automation you trust and one you have to watch.

scenes.narration: What would I not use this for? Anything where being wrong is expensive. This gives you a fast, structured, plausible first pass - and plausible is exactly the risk. It is a starting point for your judgement, not a substitute for it. Treat the output as a draft written by someone confident and occasionally wrong.
